name: Hassan Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and lead a blast-hole drill team at a large mine. I check the rig pressure and ground marks before drilling, then help newer operators learn a safe stop. My two-year technical diploma opened the door, and years on the rig taught me the feel of a binding bit. I use AI daily to sort maintenance notes, but I check the gauge before I tell anyone to move.

say: I welcome a **faster log** if safe drill staffing remains.
I use **AI notes** daily but verify pressure against the rig gauge.
think: I feel **financially steady** with four months saved and regular pay.
I want **junior practice** protected even when logging gets quicker.
do: **Lead** drilling shifts and keep physical pressure checks.
**Transfer** our usual monthly amount into savings.
**Show** the newest operator how to compare digital logs with rig gauges.
feel: **Calm** about work and bills in a mild AI future.
S0.quote: A pressure reading can look tidy in a log while the hose pulses in front of me.
fieldNote: **Daily AI use** is already established and stays checked against physical pressure readings.
**Four-month cushion** and typical pay make mild change feel manageable.
**Training juniors** is a practical concern that recurs across his answers.

steps.text: Keep leading blast-hole drilling with physical gauge checks
Continue the usual monthly savings transfer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the drill team that a faster log is welcome if it gives us more time at the rig, not fewer people on shift. I use AI daily to sort maintenance notes, but I check every pressure figure against the gauge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quiet AI outcome would be fine for our household. We have four months of expenses saved and my mine wage is steady, so the pension is a planning job rather than an emergency today. I still want junior operators to get proper time with the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading blast-hole drilling and use the same pressure checks. In the first year I would continue the monthly savings transfer and show the newest operator how to match a digital log with the rig gauge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work and our bills. I could use less typing, provided we do not turn a shortcut into a safety rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that gauge check catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pressure reading can look tidy in a log while the hose pulses in front of me. I stop the rig and ask maintenance before anyone drills another hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach the newest operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My trainee coworker Eli is quick with screens but has not felt that pulse yet. I would rather spend ten minutes beside him than repair a broken hose.

say: I expect **buying and planning** to change before drilling crews.
I want **operators** in trials before staffing is changed.
think: I see **office tasks** shrinking first, with robot effects on drilling later.
I worry **newer operators** could be excluded from paid instruction.
do: **Ask** the union steward to raise trial staffing this month.
**Test** a planning display on paid time if access is offered.
**Record** wrong hole locations against field marks.
feel: **Uneasy** about junior jobs and how the trial might shape the roster.
S1.quote: A trial without the people who drill is missing its most important check.
fieldNote: **Field marks** give him a precise test of the planning display.
**Union route** is about written staffing and safety terms, not stopping every trial.
**Own shifts** appear secure near term because drilling is physical.

steps.text: Ask the union steward to raise paid trial staffing
Test the new planning display on paid time if access is offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say software may buy parts and plan holes faster, but it cannot see a damaged hose unless somebody reports one. I would put operators on any trial group before the mine changes staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buying office may lose tasks first. My drilling crew does physical work, so our shifts should continue for a while, though slower robots could eventually reduce them. I want the union to see the trial data so new operators are not quietly left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would ask the union steward to put trial staffing and paid instruction on the meeting agenda. In the first year I would test a new planning display on paid time if the mine offers access, and record wrong hole locations against our field marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about what happens to newer workers. I am interested in the display, but I do not want the crew to learn about a cut from a rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark any hole location that puts a rig too close to an unstable edge. I would bring the field mark and screen record to the trial meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the union slow the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the steward to get safety and staffing terms in writing, not to stop a useful test. A trial without the people who drill is missing its most important check.

say: I separate **2028 planning** change from capable drill robots around 2031.
I want **paid retraining** and written shift numbers before rigs change.
think: I might lose **drilling hours** at 63 despite senior skill.
I cannot stretch **four months** saved into years of missing pay.
do: **Ask** the union to negotiate written robot-staffing terms now.
**Take** a paid remote-rig course after 2028 if offered a place.
**Apply** to a nearby mine if drilling shifts start falling.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours before a pension can be confirmed.
S2.quote: My years on the drill will not by themselves create a remote-rig seat.
fieldNote: **Age 63** at capable robots precedes any pension decision backed by household numbers.
**Four-month reserve** gives some response time but cannot replace a wage for years.
**Paid course** and nearby applications stay conditional on places and falling shifts.

steps.text: Ask the union for written robot-staffing terms
Take a paid remote-rig course if a place is offered
Apply to a nearby mine if drilling shifts begin falling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI changes planning by 2028, and capable drill robots arrive around 2031. We should bargain for paid retraining and clear shift numbers while we still run the rigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 at the robot date. I could lose drilling hours if machines handle the whole pattern, and four months saved would not replace a long wage gap. Some mines nearby might have work, but I would not count a vacancy until I saw one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the union to seek a written robot-staffing agreement and check the pension statement with my partner. In the first year after 2028 I would take a paid remote-rig course if a place is offered, and apply to a nearby mine if my shifts start falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, though there is a plan to press. My years on the drill will not by themselves create a remote-rig seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the agreement say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the number of rig shifts, paid training places and notice before a cut. I want the answers posted where every operator can see them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare pension income with our monthly bills before choosing that. My partner and I cannot live on four months of savings for years.

say: I see **2031 planning** change before drill robots around 2034.
I want **paid training** and pension figures during the extra years.
think: I might choose **fewer shifts** at 66 if pension income covers bills.
I may still need **mine wages** and a real remote-rig job.
do: **Request** course pay rules and a pension estimate this year.
**Enrol** after 2031 if a paid course place exists.
**Review** the rota before reducing drilling hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about later shifts, with time to test a course and pension.
S3.quote: I would not call a mine training promise a paid remote-rig job offer.
fieldNote: **Age 66** could make reduced hours possible, but only after pension and savings checks.
**Course place** must be paid and available; an enquiry is not counted as retraining.
**Union follow-up** remains available if promised places never open.

steps.text: Enrol in remote-rig training if a paid place exists
Wait to reduce drilling hours until pension and rota figures are checked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches planning by 2031, with capable drill robots around 2034. Five years to the first change gives us time to train operators and check whether the pension will carry older workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when robots arrive. I may choose fewer shifts if the pension and savings support it, but I could still need mine wages. I want a remote-rig option because someone has to know when a drill bit binds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mine this year for the remote-rig course pay rules and request a pension estimate. In the first year after 2031 I would enrol if the course is paid and a place exists, then review the shift rota before reducing any drilling hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the future roster, but I have enough time to check the numbers. I do not need to gamble the current wage on an unposted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a real rig, a binding bit and a safe stop included. A screen-only demonstration would leave out the hardest part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no course place opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep drilling while shifts exist and ask the union steward to raise the missing places. I would not call a mine training promise a paid remote-rig job offer.

say: I see **2036 planning** before capable drill robots around 2039.
I want **fair notice** and training terms written during the decade.
think: I hope to leave **full shifts** before robots arrive at 71.
I will check **pension income** before assuming four months saved is enough.
do: **Keep** leading safe drilling shifts for now.
**Review** pension figures yearly with my partner.
**Reduce** shifts after 2036 only if income covers bills.
feel: **Calm** about near-term work, with retirement figures still to check.
S4.quote: A recorded lesson cannot teach the feel of a bit binding.
fieldNote: **Future ages** are 68 at thinking AI and 71 at capable drill robots.
**Mentoring** is a real part of his senior work, with live stop drills for a junior.
**Four months** saved allows planning but does not substitute for pension income.

steps.text: Keep leading safe drilling shifts on the current rota
Wait to reduce shifts until pension income covers household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI changes planning in 2036 and capable drill robots follow around 2039. A decade gives the mine plenty of time to write fair notice and training terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the first date and 71 at the second. I hope to leave full drilling shifts before robots arrive, but I will check the pension rather than assume it. Four months saved is useful for a transition, not a lifetime of rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading safe drilling shifts and review the pension each year with my partner. In the first year after 2036 I would compare pension income with household bills and reduce shifts only if the figures work, while showing a junior operator the rig stop drills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, with the pension still on my mind. There is time to put real terms around the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would learn the stop drills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would train my junior coworker Mara on a live rig with a qualified operator beside us. A recorded lesson cannot teach the feel of a bit binding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid drilling shifts if they are offered and consider a nearby mine if they are not. I would rather keep a wage than call myself retired too soon.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable drill robots around 2031 could cut my hours before I have confirmed a pension. A written staffing agreement, paid remote-rig training and notice before cuts would help. I want the union and operators at the trial table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who shows a new operator what a binding bit feels like. A machine log can record pressure, but a worker still needs hands-on teaching to stop safely.

headlineQuote: A machine log can record pressure, but a worker still needs hands-on teaching to stop safely.
portrait: **Hassan, 58**, leads blast-hole drilling and checks digital maintenance notes against rig pressure and ground marks.
**Typical pay** and four months saved give some room to plan while retirement income remains unconfirmed.
**Daily AI use** coexists with physical checks; he wants operators and the union inside machine trials.
**Fast AGI** makes him anxious because 2028 planning change precedes capable drill robots around 2031.
**Longer warning** lets him seek paid remote-rig training and verify pension income before cutting shifts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives the shortest time before capable drill robots may reduce his hours at 63.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing terms** and notice before cuts would let operators plan.
**Paid remote-rig training** with offered places would help him keep earning if work changes.
